item.text:
Consider the class \(\mathcal C\) of subsets of the full product whose membership depends on only countably many coordinates. Show that \(\mathcal C\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra:

- complements retain the same coordinate set;
- for a countable union, take the countable union \(I=\bigcup_n I_n\) of all coordinate sets and lift each corresponding \(t_n\) to the product over \(I\).

Every generating cylinder \(\pi_i^{-1}(A)\) belongs to \(\mathcal C\), since it depends only on the singleton \(\{i\}\). The product \(\sigma\)-algebra is generated by these coordinate cylinders, so every measurable \(s\) lies in \(\mathcal C\). Unpacking this gives a countable \(I\) and \(t\) with
\[
s=(\operatorname{restrict}_I)^{-1}(t).
\]

The key mechanism is that \(\sigma\)-algebra generation uses only countable operations, matching closure of countable coordinate dependence under countable unions.
